title: Is Public Sector a Better Place for Moms to Work? Exploring Sector Difference in Child Penalties on Women
authors: Fangda Ding; Yifan Chen
affiliations: Department of Politics and Public Administration The University of Hong Kong Hong Kong SAR China; School of International and Public Affairs The China Institute for Urban Governance The Shanghai Research Center for Innovation and Policy Evaluation Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai China
abstract: ABSTRACT With commonly stabler and more flexible working environment, is public sector a better place for moms to work? Theorizing child penalties from sector difference perspective, we argue that childbirth may cause less gender gaps in unemployment and earnings but greater gender disparities in working time commitments in the public sector since job stability and family‐friendliness may form gender norms that depreciate women's work in the public sector. We test our hypotheses by employing event study designs using data from China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022). We found that women public employees experienced smaller child penalties in unemployment and earnings while greater child penalties in working hours than private counterparts, which can be explained by greater family responsibilities and spousal depreciation of women's jobs after childbirth. This paper advances theories of gender equity in public administration by proposing distinct child penalties in the public sector that challenges conventional beliefs.

title: A Public Philosophy for Public Administration in Times of Democratic Crisis
authors: Curtis Ventriss; Tina Nabatchi
affiliations: University of Vermont Burlington Vermont USA; Syracuse University Syracuse New York USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Public administration is at the center of the global democratic crisis. Meeting this challenge requires more than managerial and analytic competence—it requires a public philosophy grounded in the first principles of democratic ethos. We offer such a philosophy, drawing on four seminal thinkers whose concepts reflect the conditions public administrators face in times of democratic crisis. Judith Shklar's liberalism of fear establishes a negative obligation to refuse cruelty and resist its institutionalization. Alasdair MacIntyre's internal goods of practice create a positive obligation to cultivate virtue and protect the integrity of administrative practice. Isaiah Berlin's agony of choice obligates administrators to acknowledge irreducible value conflicts and their consequential impact on democratic life. Hannah Arendt's enlarged mentality provides a framework for thinking across perspectives so that judgment under conflict becomes democratically defensible. Together, these concepts form a public philosophy for public administration with practical significance for administrative judgment, organizational culture, and institutional courage.

title: Reply to Kettl: Public Administration and the Shifting Competing Forces of Accountability
authors: Charles Wise
affiliations: School of Government and Public Policy University of Arizona Tucson Arizona USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The accountability context for how public administrators operate has shifted markedly and has become much more volatile. This shift has placed new and some conflicting demands on public administrators to demonstrate their accountability to various competing governmental actors and has complicated policy and program implementation. The changed context, its causes, and the resultant challenges are analyzed and discussed. Questions are presented for public administration research to help public administrators deal with the challenges.

title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
authors: Mayur Joshi; Ning Su; Mark Zbaracki
affiliations: University of Ottawa Telfer School of Management, Business Analytics and Information Systems, Ottawa, Canada; Western University Ivey Business School, General Management, Strategy & Information Systems, London, Canada; Western University, Ivey Business School, London, Canada
abstract: Predictive AI models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict, but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge.

title: Colleagues that work together move together: How co-moving among newcomers affects individual and team performance.
authors: Emma Y. Zhao; Catherine Shea; Siyuan Li
affiliations: University of Virginia, McIntire School of Commerce, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States; Carnegie Mellon University Tepper School of Business, Organizational Behavior and Theory, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States; William & Mary Raymond A Mason School of Business, Mason School of Business, Williamsburg, Virginia, United States
abstract: As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multi-theory, and multi-period model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience which they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, though these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: while co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.

title: Legal Chameleons: Political Ideology, Institutional Histories, and Firms’ Management of Identity Cues
authors: Yong Kim; Jose Nicolas Uribe; Maxim Sytch
affiliations: Texas A&M University, Department of Management, College Station, Texas, United States; Indiana University, Management and Entrepreneurship, Bloomington, Indiana, United States; University of Michigan-Ann Arbor, Management and Organizations, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States
abstract: This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post-hoc analyses reveal that adjusting the ethnic composition of external legal teams attenuates the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes in conservative courts. These findings contribute to research on liability of foreignness by identifying agent selection as a specific mitigation mechanism in evaluative arenas.

title: Reconceptualizing Network Change: Robustness and Resilience of Interorganizational Networks
authors: Maxim Sytch; Sukanya Roy; Pavel I. Zhelyazkov
affiliations: University of Michigan, Management and Organizations, Ross School of Business, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States; University of Michigan, Ross School of Business, Management and Organizations, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Management, Kowloon, Hong Kong
abstract: Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, and cascading partner failures, and can rapidly reconfigure whole‑network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness–resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass pre‑shock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness–resilience perspective opens for the study of network change.

title: Optimizing Input Data Collection for Ranking and Selection
authors: Eunhye Song; Taeho Kim
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, Industrial and Systems Engineering, Atlanta, Georgia, United States; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics, and Operations Management, Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: We study a ranking and selection (R&S) problem when all solutions share common parametric Bayesian input models updated with the data collected from multiple independent data-generating sources. Our objective is to identify the best system by designing a sequential sampling algorithm that collects input and simulation data given a budget. We adopt the most probable best (MPB) as the estimator of the optimum and show that its posterior probability of optimality converges to one at an exponential rate as the sampling budget increases. Assuming that the input parameters belong to a finite set, we characterize the optimal static sampling ratios for input and simulation data that maximize the convergence rate. Using these ratios as guidance, we propose the optimal sampling algorithm for R&S (OSAR) that achieves the optimal ratios almost surely in the limit. We further extend OSAR by adopting the kernel ridge regression to improve the simulation output mean prediction. This not only improves OSAR’s finite-sample performance, but also lets us tackle the case where the input parameters lie in a continuous space with a strong consistency guarantee for finding the optimum. We numerically demonstrate that OSAR outperforms a state-of-the-art competitor.

title: Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation for Ad Measurement
authors: Brett R. Gordon; Robert Moakler; Florian Zettelmeyer
affiliations: Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208; Ads Research, Meta, Menlo Park, California 94025; Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208; and National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138
abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provide the most credible estimates of advertising incrementality but are difficult to scale. We propose Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation (PIE), which reframes ad measurement as a campaign-level prediction problem. PIE uses a sample of RCTs to learn a mapping from campaign features to causal effects, then applies it to campaigns not run as RCTs. Because the RCTs identify the causal effects, PIE can incorporate post-determined features—campaign-level aggregates such as test-group outcomes, exposure rates, and last-click conversions, computed after campaign completion. These metrics reflect the consumer behaviors that generate treatment effects, so they carry predictive information about incrementality, even though they would be invalid controls in a causal model. Using 2,226 Meta ad experiments, PIE achieves an out-of-sample [Formula: see text] for incremental conversions per dollar, compared with [Formula: see text] for industry-standard seven-day last-click attribution. In a decision-making framework, PIE disagrees with RCT-based decisions in only 8%–12% of campaigns, compared with 12%–20% for last-click attribution. We conclude that PIE can help scale causal measurement from a limited number of RCTs to a large set of nonexperimental campaigns. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. title: Helping Oneself by Helping a Rival: Social-Media Platforms’ Policies on Enabling Features for Influencers
authors: Yan Zhu; Jianqing Chen; Srinivasan Raghunathan
affiliations: The University of Texas at Dallas, Jindal School of Management, Richardson, Texas, 75080-3021, United States; The University of Texas at Dallas, Jindal School of Management, Richardson, Texas, United States; University of Texas at Dallas, Information Systems, Richardson, United States
abstract: Social-media platforms and influencers are often seen as collaborators. However, both rely primarily on advertising services, introducing a competitive dimension to their relationship. As the dominant players in this relationship, platforms have used design features, which they control, to manage this dynamic. Some platforms have adopted an antagonistic approach by disabling certain features (e.g., clickable shopping-related hyperlinks) for influencers, while others take a more cooperative stance, allowing influencers to use these features for free or for a fee. We develop a game-theoretic model to explore the competition between the two parties and study the platform’s decision to enable or disable a feature that enhances the effectiveness of an influencer’s service. We show that even when the platform cannot charge the influencers for using the feature, it can still benefit if the advertisers’ valuation of the platform’s service is not significantly lower than that of the influencer’s service. While enabling the feature may result in a loss of market share, the platform can potentially offset this loss by raising its prices. A win–win situation for the platform and the influencer may come at the expense of some advertisers, suggesting the platform’s helping the influencer can lead to a “collusive” outcome, despite the competition for advertisers. If the platform can charge a fee for using the feature, it should always enable the feature at an appropriate fee, as this will benefit the platform. The additional fee revenue may come with no change in the platform’s advertising revenue, with an increase in the advertising revenue, or at the expense of some advertising revenue. The platform strategically uses the fee to influence the influencer’s service offering, which affects the platform’s revenue mix under the new business model.

title: From trade-off to paradox: a configurational theorizing and “quantum” approach to the resilience–sustainability tension in global sourcing
authors: Giacomo Grassi; Stefano Elia; Cristina Di Stefano; Michela Guida; Federico Caniato
abstract: Abstract Global sourcing is increasingly caught between two persistent pressures: to be sustainable and resilient. While this relationship is often framed as a trade-off, we draw on paradox theory to conceptualize it as a persistent paradox, especially for MNEs coordinating complex supplier networks. Most paradox research addresses either how tensions are embedded in organizational systems or how they are socially constructed by managers, but rarely both. Drawing on the "quantum" approach to paradox, we bridge these ontological and epistemological perspectives, arguing that the resilience–sustainability tension is rooted in the structure of global sourcing systems and made salient through how managers interpret and combine sourcing decisions. Following a configurational roadmap of three stages—scoping, linking, and naming—we theorize five systemic sourcing factors (location choice, supplier redundancy, inventory buffer, green certification, and the sustainability premium) and examine how they are evaluated by 72 Italian procurement managers through a factorial survey, a fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and interviews. Managers favor coherent bundles over standalone levers, combining certification-based sustainability assurance alongside resilience-oriented levers such as proximity, redundancy, and buffers. We conceptualize three archetypal sourcing logics— integrator , resilience-first , and cost-only —offering managers a practical vocabulary for framing and legitimating sourcing choices when both pressures collide.

title: Transaction Hazards Through Ideological Filters: How CEO Political Ideology Influences Vertical Integration Decisions
authors: Holly Loncarich; Mirzokhidjon Abdurakhmonov; Madison L. Schnacker
affiliations: Kansas State University; University of Nebraska-Lincoln
abstract: Why do firms facing similar transaction environments adopt different boundary structures? Transaction cost theory (TCT) predicts governance choices based on transaction hazards, but persistent heterogeneity in vertical integration suggests that such efficiency-based explanations are incomplete. We examine whether CEO political ideology is associated with systematic variation in firm boundary decisions. Drawing on research on political ideology and strategic leadership, we argue that ideological orientations shape how executives evaluate and prioritize governance trade-offs. Using a panel of 1,198 U.S. public firms from 2001 to 2020 and a firm fixed-effects design exploiting CEO successions, we find that firms led by more conservative CEOs exhibit higher levels of vertical integration. This relationship weakens when asset specificity is high and when industries are more concentrated but is not amplified by demand volatility. Our findings suggest that firm boundaries reflect not only transaction conditions but also systematic differences in executive decision-making.

title: Impostors in paradise: Toxic inclusion in elite doctoral education
authors: Adél Pásztor
affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest, Hungary
abstract: Elite universities have expanded access, but the terms of recognition after admission remain stratified. This article develops the concept of toxic inclusion to capture a form of institutional incorporation in which formal admission coexists with situationally negotiated recognition after entry. Drawing on interviews with Eastern European doctoral students at a prestigious transnational European graduate school, the analysis shows how admission does not itself secure legitimacy, but relocates inequality into everyday processes of evaluation, interaction, and self-positioning where the legibility of prior trajectories within transnational evaluative frameworks becomes consequential. The findings identify four mechanisms through which inequality is reconfigured after admission: legitimacy on loan, epistemic silencing, impostor work and the morality of belonging. While not uniformly experienced, these dynamics show how recognition is negotiated across symbolic, epistemic, affective and moral dimensions, reshaping inequality beyond admission.

title: Misidentification, confusion and uncertainty: How working-class youth interpret their class identities
authors: Amit Singh
affiliations: Social Research Institute, University College London, England, UK
abstract: This paper investigates how predominantly white, working-class young people (aged 16–22 years old) in London, Rochdale and Morecambe conceptualise class within their lives. Despite facing poverty,inequality and exclusion, these individuals frequently misidentify their class, not out of defensiveness, but out of confusion and uncertainty because the language of class does not resonate with them, with the majority of respondents failing to identify as working-class in clear terms. This occurs against the backdrop of highly visible, politicised narratives pertaining to a ‘left behind’, exclusively white, working-class who are said to live in places like Rochdale and Morecambe. The research contributes to the understanding of how young people interpret their class identities through demonstrating that class is shaped by local dynamics in the context of class decomposition and demobilisation. Ultimately, this paper argues that a lack of awareness about class as identity, did not mean that these young people did not understand wider experiences of inequality and hardship. Rather, there is a disjuncture between how class is lived and how class identities are claimed.

title: ‘This is not what science is’: Researchers’ perspectives on doing decolonial research in Flemish (Belgian) higher education
authors: Elif Lootens; Peter A. J. Stevens; Bart Van de Putte
affiliations: Ghent University, Belgium
abstract: Despite the sociological attention paid to the role of racism in producing racial inequalities in universities, few studies have examined epistemic coloniality and marginalization at the level of social knowledge within academia. Foregrounding the university context, where anti-colonial knowledge is simultaneously marginalized, this article asks what the possibilities are for decolonial critiques of knowledge within universities. Based on interviews with racialized PhD researchers of colour, this study examines the possibilities and challenges of conducting decolonial research within a university context. We argue that the epistemic frameworks of social sciences are intrinsically racialized, fostering exclusionary modes of thought and practices that align with racial and socio-geographical lines. Second, this study reveals how dominant conceptions of scientific validity and neutrality in social sciences sustain the epistemic status quo, contributing to ‘epistemic coloniality’ by invalidating decolonial researchers.

title: The unintended effect of monetary incentives on shirking in manufacturer–reseller relationships
authors: Matthew J. Robson; Claude Obadia; Constantine S. Katsikeas
affiliations: Cardiff Business School, Cardiff University , ,; ESCE International Business School, Omnes Education , ,; Leeds University Business School, University of Leeds , ,
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how temporal changes in manufacturer monetary incentives influence reseller behavior within manufacturer–reseller relationships. We theorize, using agency theory, and examine empirically how the manufacturer's incentive changes have complex and unintended effects on the reseller's shirking, ultimately shaping the manufacturer's economic performance. Design/methodology/approach We test our hypotheses on the effect of incentives using data from two successive surveys of exporting manufacturers in partnerships with foreign resellers, together with archival sources. Findings We observe a U-shaped relationship of monetary-incentive changes with shirking. The results reveal that when monetary incentives are decreasing (left-side of the U), their effect on reseller shirking is negative, but when they are increasing (right-side of the U), they can have a positive effect on shirking. The U-shaped relationship steepens when import market GDP growth is high. Practical implications Manufacturer managers should scrutinize and even resist reseller requests to increase monetary incentives because in most cases, the intended positive act of boosting incentives leads to an unintended increase in reseller shirking and a reduction in manufacturer performance. Originality/value We adopt a novel approach that examines intertemporal changes in monetary incentives within manufacturer–reseller relationships. Our findings add to modern thinking on agency theory, which views the level of convergence between the principal's and the agent's economic interests as a dynamic process shaped by wider considerations pertaining to relationship status.

title: Within‐Sector Job Mobility and Worker Outcomes in England's Adult Social Care Sector
authors: Akbar Ullah; William Whittaker; Carol Woodhams; Carol Atkinson
affiliations: Health Organisation, Policy and Economics (HOPE) The University of Manchester Manchester UK; NIHR Applied Research Collaboration Greater Manchester The University of Manchester Manchester UK; Institute of Population Health University of Liverpool Liverpool UK; Surrey Business School University of Surrey Guildford UK; Centre for Decent Work and Productivity Manchester Metropolitan University Manchester UK
abstract: ABSTRACT England's adult social care sector faces persistently high staff turnover. This article examines the effects of individual‐level within‐sector job mobility on hourly pay and working hours and identifies the employer types and contractual arrangements that attract such mobility. Using an event‐study difference‐in‐differences (DiD) design, we show that job mobility increases hourly pay by 4.5% in the first year, rising to 6.1% after 5 years. Instrumental variable analyses either corroborate the DiD estimates or show higher impacts. Mobility also raises weekly working hours and reduces the likelihood of 0‐h contracts by around 7.0 percentage points. Employer‐specific wage premia account for nearly half of observed pay gains, whereas worker–employer match effects play little role. Workers predominantly move to higher paying employers—particularly local authorities and community‐based services—into fixed‐hours contracts and out of direct care roles. Moves into 0‐h contracts result in modest pay losses. Men experience larger pay gains from mobility than women.

title: How Strategic Leaders Drive Firms in Ecosystems: Envisioning Value, Orchestrating Knowledge, and Shifting Roles
authors: Paolo Aversa; Carmelo Cennamo; Ambra Mazzelli; Gianni Lorenzoni
affiliations: King's College London; Copenhagen Business School; SKEMA Business School, Université Côte d'Azur (GREDEG); University of Bologna
abstract: Abstract Research on business ecosystems has illuminated how ecosystems emerge, evolve, and transform, revealing ecosystem‐level dynamics and the central actors that orchestrate them. Yet, it is individual firms that continuously attempt to establish and shift the roles they play within ecosystems through the vision and choices of their strategic leaders. How do strategic leaders drive these shifts? Through a longitudinal case study of Dallara Automobili (1972–2025), we trace how the CEO's prior professional experience shaped an evolving theory of value – a set of conjectures about how value should be created that guided the development of organizational routines enabling progressively more expansive knowledge orchestration. This process shifted Dallara from a peripheral component supplier to a boundary‐spanning knowledge orchestrator. Our recursive process model theorizes how the leader's conjectures drive firm role shifts within an ecosystem: experience shapes the leader's theory of value, which drives organizational routines and knowledge orchestration; knowledge orchestration, in turn, redefines the firm's ecosystem role. Ecosystem responses then feed back, augmenting prior experience and, in turn, refining the theory of value so that each round operates at a broader scope. We contribute to ecosystem research by identifying knowledge orchestration as the mechanism through which a leader's theory of value translates into shifts in the firm's role and by showing how this process unfolds recursively as ecosystem responses reshape the leader's conjectures.

title: Navigating the Digital Capital Paradox: Whether and How It Impacts Export Intensity
authors: Yuge Dong; Xinming He; Markus Blut
affiliations: Shanghai Business School 2271 West Zhong Shan Rd. Shanghai 200235 China; Durham University Business School Durham University Durham DH1 1SL UK
abstract: Abstract Established firms are making substantial investments in digital capital (DC) – that is, capitalized software and systems – to enhance exports, yet they often face perplexing, even negative returns. We argue that this tension reflects an inherent resource–liability paradox, where DC acts simultaneously as a strategic resource and an operational liability. Drawing on paradox theory, we examine a framework that specifies how dynamic capability and external institutional frictions shape the outcomes of this persistent tension. Using longitudinal data of Chinese listed firms, we find that the unmanaged paradox manifests as a significant negative impact on export intensity. We theorize and demonstrate that a strong firm‐level digital orientation (DO) enables firms to reconcile the tension and reverse the negative effect. Informal institutional distance exacerbates the core paradox, while formal distance does not, highlighting the primacy of implicit, cognitive frictions over explicit, regulatory costs. Our study enriches the export literature and paradox theory by identifying DO as a higher level dynamic capability and advancing understanding of contextual intensification by disentangling the distinct roles of formal and informal institutional distances. Hence, realizing DC's international value depends not on the investment itself, but on the firm's ability to manage these internal contradictions within challenging institutional contexts.

title: China's Initial Public Offering Peer‐based Valuation: Market versus Regulatory Pricing Regimes
authors: Wei Zhang; Xiong Xiong; Guanying Wang; Nianhang Xu
affiliations: School of Finance Tianjin University of Finance and Economics Tianjin China; Laboratory of Computation and Analytics of Complex Management Systems (CACMS) Tianjin University Tianjin China; College of Management and Economics Tianjin University Tianjin China; School of Business Renmin University of China Beijing China
abstract: Abstract In 2014, China's initial public offering (IPO) valuation regime shifted from market‐based pricing to a regulatory system with a de facto 23× P/E ratio cap. This institutional change provides a compelling setting to examine how institutional constraints affect valuation efficiency and information transmission. Using a sample of IPOs and hand‐collected peer firms, we document that regulated IPOs are systematically undervalued by 42–56.9% relative to their peers. Their valuations negatively predict post‐IPO returns, while market‐priced IPOs exhibit no such pattern. A low‐minus‐high price‐to‐value strategy yields annualized abnormal returns of 15.6% for IPOs under regulatory pricing, with no comparable profits under market pricing. These effects appear to operate through two interconnected channels: corporate competitiveness and stock price informativeness. Rather than reflecting costly signalling, constrained valuation serves as an information revelation mechanism of firm quality. Our findings provide novel evidence on how institutional frictions shape information transmission beyond conventional signalling incentives.

authors: Stephanie Majerowicz; Román Andrés Zárate
affiliations: Escuela de Gobierno, Universidad de los Andes; University of Toronto Department of Economics,
abstract: Abstract This paper studies the impact of MOOC certificates on labor market outcomes using a Coursera initiative that offered free certificates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Although eligibility for free certificates was randomized, course completion rates were low-only 6.2% of eligible participants completed at least one course-so we rely on an event-study design to estimate the effects of receiving a certificate. The results show that MOOC certificates increases formal employment by about 5 percentage points, with larger impacts among participants who were not employed at baseline and those from low-income households, and no clear differences by gender. These gains are concentrated in employment at larger firms and in economic sectors aligned with the course content. Overall, while MOOCs have the potential to improve employment outcomes, additional interventions appear necessary to increase course completion rates.

title: Heterogeneous patience, population growth, and wealth accumulation
authors: Stéphane Bouché; Mikhail Pakhnin
affiliations: University of the Balearic Islands Department of Applied Economics, , Palma ,
abstract: Abstract We study a neoclassical growth model with population growth and heterogeneous agents. The model can be interpreted as either a Ramsey model with heterogeneous discounting and entry of new agents with zero endowments or an OLG model with infinitely-lived agents with different discount factors. We prove that, in the unique stationary equilibrium, agents other than the most patient may hold capital. Introducing public debt, a labor income tax, or a capital subsidy allows more agent types to save, reducing inequality among agents with different discount factors while increasing inequality among agents with the same discount factor entered in different periods.

title: Metric capital: how academic indicators become interactional resource
authors: Łukasz Remisiewicz
abstract: Abstract This article develops a sociological theory of how academic indicators acquire force in academic life. Based on Randall Collins’s interaction ritual theory, it distinguishes three analytically separate layers that are often conflated in studies of bibliometrics: reception traces, valuation tokens, and metric capital. Academic interactions leave traces in the form of citations, mentions, and article downloads. Selected ones are then stabilized by digital infrastructures, which reduce them to tokens by collecting, certifying, and making them internally comparable. Individual academics accumulate these tokens into a portfolio of objectified symbols that can be mobilized in further interactions—both informally and formally. In this way, they constitute a form of capital. It is activated through three mechanisms. First, it influences the course of interaction before it begins (pre-entrainment), is transferable through structural holes, and also allows for the closure of discussions during evaluation rituals where diverse evaluation cultures or low competence in assessing the quality of work exist. Metric capital can be separated from a scientist’s informal reputation within the scientific community in various ways. The article thus proposes to expand the discussion about measures from the question of what they represent to the question of how they interactively shape the scientific order.

title: Moving towards decolonizing health professions education research: an analysis of global network patterns and equity implications
authors: Peerasit Sitthirat; Seksan Yoadsanit; Phuphinyo Limchantra; Kanjaree Suppawittaya; Suttithan Suwannoppakun; Piwat Suppawittaya; Phanuwich Kaewkamjornchai; Somsak Chunharas
abstract: Abstract Colonialism has left a lasting remnant in global academic community, with research contributions and authorship historically concentrated among high-income countries. This imbalance has made decolonization in research a global agenda aimed at rebalancing power relations across the community. Nevertheless, traditional bibliometric tools remain unable to capture such underlying power dynamics. This study proposes leveraging social network analysis (SNA) to examine community architecture and promote inclusivity in health professions education (HPE) research. We analyzed peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2024 in leading HPE journals, extracting country-level co-authorship data from Scopus. SNA metrics, particularly small world coefficient and centrality, were used to assess collaboration structures, integration patterns, and power dynamics, capturing how power is distributed across the network. The analysis revealed an expanding–centralized pattern: although the research community has expanded globally, with more countries contributing, the overall network structure has remained hierarchical. The network’s small-worldness declined, indicating growing concentration of power within the network core, while stable centrality showed that dominant players have remained consistent throughout the decade. Despite an increasing number of nodes suggesting broader participation, power became increasingly centralized rather than distributed toward the periphery, suggesting the global network remains structurally inequitable and epistemic colonization may still persist. Systemic reforms in research infrastructure, nationally and globally, and in journal policies are needed to enable greater inclusivity. SNA offers critical insight into the structural imbalances that must be monitored to guide process toward achieving an equitable global research ecosystem.

title: Flow‐Driven ESG Returns
authors: PHILIPPE VAN DER BECK
abstract: ABSTRACT I show that the recent returns to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing are strongly driven by price impact from flows toward ESG portfolios. Using data on trades, I estimate the market's ability to accommodate ESG flows, which is given by the elasticity of substitution between ESG and other stocks. I show that every dollar flowing toward a representative ESG portfolio increases the market value of ESG stocks by $0.8. The growing institutional flows into the ESG portfolio are the main driver of ESG returns and have caused an annual flow‐driven return of 1.9%. In the absence of flows, ESG stocks would not have outperformed the market from 2012 to 2023.

title: The Financial Premium
authors: JENS DICK‐NIELSEN; PETER FELDHÜTTER; DAVID LANDO
abstract: ABSTRACT We show that bonds issued by financial firms have higher spreads than bonds issued by industrial firms with the same rating and maturity, a difference that we refer to as the financial premium. Over the period 1987 to 2020, in the United States, this premium is 43 basis points on average, with the premium higher for lower ratings, higher during financial crises, and increasing in bond beta. We derive a model that explains the financial premium: banks hold diversified portfolios of nonfinancial debt, and bank debt therefore reflects more systematic risk than nonfinancial debt.

title: Feedback and Contagion through Distressed Competition
authors: HUI CHEN; WINSTON WEI DOU; HONGYE GUO; YAN JI
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms tend to compete more aggressively when facing financial distress. This intensified competition reduces profit margins, pushing them further into distress and adversely affecting their industry peers. To study such feedback and contagion effects, we incorporate strategic competition in a dynamic model with long‐term defaultable debt, exploring various peer interactions such as predation and price wars. The feedback effect represents a novel source of financial distress costs associated with leverage, which helps explain the negative profitability‐leverage relation across industries. Owing to the contagion effect, firms' optimal leverage is often excessively high from an industry perspective, undermining the industry's financial stability.

title: Generative AI and Firm Values
authors: ANDREA L. EISFELDT; GREGOR SCHUBERT; MIAO BEN ZHANG; BLEDI TASKA
abstract: ABSTRACT How do recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) affect firm value? We construct the first measure of firms' workforce exposures to Generative AI and show that an “Artificial‐Minus‐Human” portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks following the release of ChatGPT. The labor‐exposure effect is more pronounced for firms with greater data assets and is distinct from the effect of firms' product exposures to AI. We assess whether exposed workforces are substituted or complemented by Generative AI based on whether their exposed tasks are core or supplemental. Examining firms' labor demand and profitability following the release of ChatGPT supports a labor‐technology substitution channel.

title: From Text to Beta: Macroeconomic Disclosures and Firm-Level Systematic Risk
authors: Cameron Holstead; Alon Kalay; Gil Sadka; Federico Siano
affiliations: RPC Consulting; Michigan State University; The University of Texas at Dallas
abstract: ABSTRACT Using news text from The Wall Street Journal and macroeconomic disclosures in 10-K filings, we address the challenge of characterizing both time-varying aggregate risks and firm-level risk exposures. We develop a disclosure-based measure of systematic risk that (1) reveals salient macro risks in each period, (2) provides a text-based estimate of earnings exposure to these risks, and (3) explains the cross-section of stock returns. We also show that macro disclosures are pervasive across the annual report, grow over time, vary with the business cycle, and exhibit within-firm variation, consistent with the time-varying nature of systematic risk exposure. Overall, disclosures yield transparent and economically interpretable estimates of firm-level systematic risk. Data Availability: Data are obtained from SEC filings, Bureau of Economic Analysis, The Wall Street Journal, Compustat, CRSP, I/B/E/S. JEL Classifications: E31; E32; G11; G12; M21; M41.

title: Choosing the Stage: The Strategic Role of Disclosure Venues in Guidance Revisions
authors: Akash Chattopadhyay; Nayana Reiter; Mani Sethuraman
affiliations: Rotman School of Management University of Toronto Toronto Ontario Canada; Cornell University Ithaca New York USA
abstract: ABSTRACT When managers revise earnings guidance between earnings announcements, they choose not only what to disclose but also where to disclose—in a standalone release, a guidance call, an investor conference, or an analyst/investor (A/I) day. These venues differ in audience, format, and visibility, raising the question of whether venue choice is a strategic communication decision. In a large sample of unbundled revisions, we find that managers use calls for relatively large negative revisions and when litigation risk is higher and that they use conferences and A/I days for smaller revisions and when analyst disagreement is greater. Textual analysis reveals that calls feature cautious, litigious language for both upward and downward revisions, whereas conference and A/I day communications remain optimistic. In line with these framing differences, calls are associated with amplified reaction to negative news and are followed by more favorable earnings surprises, suggestive of effective expectation management, whereas conferences and A/I days are associated with muted reactions and reduced analyst dispersion and are followed by less favorable surprises. Our findings suggest that venue choice is a dimension of disclosure strategy for managers and an informative signal for investors.

title: When Can Clientelism Serve Democratic Ends? A Democratic Theory of Distributive Politics
authors: SAMUEL ELY BAGG; UDIT BHATIA
affiliations: University of South Carolina; King’s College London
abstract: This article employs normative democratic theory to examine a counterintuitive suggestion raised repeatedly by empirical scholars of clientelism: namely, that practices of particularistic exchange might sometimes serve democratic ends. Certainly, most particularistic practices are widely agreed to undermine democracy, on both intrinsic and instrumental grounds. Yet some observers resist blanket condemnation—and in particular, many highlight the redeeming democratic virtues of certain practices that seem to facilitate collective organization among disempowered groups. Drawing on “realist” approaches to democratic theory, we vindicate this basic insight while clarifying its scope conditions. Countervailing power is a crucial democratic priority, and programmatic methods of promoting it sometimes face serious obstacles: as when clientelist practices are deeply entrenched, or incumbents capture the tools of programmatic competition. Under such conditions, we conclude, democracy-seeking leaders may justifiably employ particularistic practices to promote countervailing power—but only if they respect five constraints tethering them strictly to that goal.

title: The Idea of a Counter-Structure: Rethinking Collective Action against Climate Injustice
authors: JONATHAN MASIN-PETERS
affiliations: Harvard University
abstract: This article argues that addressing the structural injustices of climate change requires rethinking collective action. Disruptive and prefigurative politics are often treated as separate collective action repertoires, but I argue that a just energy transition requires that they work in tandem. To capture this interaction, I propose the idea of “counter-structural” collective action, in which disruptive protest creates windows of opportunity that prefigurative alternatives can then fill. Through analysis of two UK climate movements, Transition Towns (TTs) and Camps for Climate Action (CCA), I show how activists reconfigure structural elements to build new, carbon-free social and political forms. The theory of counter-structural action provides a framework for assessing the empirical cases. The cases, in turn, illustrate a broader conception of collective action that better reflects the social theory grounding structural injustice. Together, the theory and cases support the dual aims of climate justice: challenging fossil-fuel path dependence and advancing egalitarianism.

title: Teaching the past, informing the present? School history education and attitudes toward foreign countries
authors: Soyoung Lee; Jeongmin Park
affiliations: Assistant Professor, Department of Political Science Yale University New Haven Connecticut USA; Postdoctoral Prize Fellow, Department of Politics Oxford University Nuffield College Oxford UK
abstract: Abstract How does school history education emphasizing past grievances with other countries impact attitudes toward conflict and cooperation with the countries today? We examine this question using original data from 34 classrooms across 17 high schools in Seoul, South Korea. We first test whether exposure to anti‐Japanese content in school history education negatively impacts students' attitudes toward cooperation with Japan. We then compare how the attitudes of students educated with a more pro‐US textbook differ from those using a more anti‐US one. We find that school history education influenced what historical events students believed as “facts” and their evaluation of historical events. However, the effect on students' historical memories did not by itself automatically translate into corresponding attitudes toward present‐day Japan or the United States. Our findings offer various implications for studies on international rivalries and historical memories, as well as for debates on the political effects of school education.
